entities.name: Ten Commandments
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Ten Commandments, also known as the Decalogue, are a set of ethical directives traditionally attributed to divine origin, believed to have been delivered by God to Moses on Mount Sinai around 1446 BCE, according to biblical chronology. This foundational text is pivotal not only in Judaism but also in Christianity and Islam, marking a significant moment in the development of moral and legal codes across cultures. The versions of the Ten Commandments found in the Hebrew Bible, particularly in Exodus 20:1–17 and Deuteronomy 5:6–21, reflect a complex interplay of religious and societal norms that have influenced millions over millennia.

The core events surrounding the Ten Commandments involve the Israelites' exodus from Egypt, a narrative central to Jewish identity and theology. Following their liberation, Moses ascended Mount Sinai, where, as described in Exodus, God inscribed the commandments on stone tablets. This act established a covenant between God and the Israelites, outlining their obligations and moral responsibilities. The commandments themselves address fundamental ethical issues such as murder, theft, and fidelity, serving as a covenantal framework that shaped the legal and moral landscapes of emerging societies.

The legacy of the Ten Commandments is profound, having influenced not only religious thought but also legal systems and moral philosophies throughout history. The commandments have been interpreted and reinterpreted, impacting various legal codes, including those in Western civilization. Their ripple effects are evident in modern discussions of ethics and law, as secular and religious leaders alike continue to reference them when addressing moral issues. As noted by historian Jacob Neusner, 'The Decalogue is the foundation of all law and morality in the Western world,' underscoring its enduring relevance and significance.
